Part 1 of llm-dlc/loops/lib-architecture-fast-follow.md. Three readers of the checker's --json output answered differently for the same bytes: for the first established row of example 359's selector record with only wire_version changed to 999, the ordinary decoder refused it while the native-selector check read it as established and the benchmark scored it correct; a stated.bounds.complete of the string "false" was established through Python's truthiness; and a process that exited with 2 beside a verified payload was scored correct. lib/src/proof_wire.rs now owns what prove --json and equivalence --json print (the wire version, the envelope, the exit as the maximum over a run's rows), with the command line as its caller. lib/python/jvmcontract_io.py is the one Python reader, standard library only, and keeps three questions apart: whether the bytes decode, whether the process ended as the command ends, and (the consumer's own) whether the evidence qualifies, for which it offers typed access where a missing or mistyped field is unknown.

Switched to it: ordinary ingestion (checker_output.py keeps its names and reads through it; an unreadable outcome's reason now names what the reader refused), the live native-selector check, the validation of archived selector records, and lib/benchmark/run.py, which the solver comparison reads through. A benchmark case must print its one row; a kill, an unknown version, a mistyped decision field, exit 2 and an exit that contradicts the verdict earn no score, and a valid refutation is still correct at exit 1. A new selector row records its wire version and a new record names both rule files.

A regression check under --cache now says what it did with each changed helper as data (the outcome's helpers: callee, action, the proof's claim key and whether it was found in the cache, a summary's reads and facts, a reason code). The notes in the output are rendered from the decision, word for word what they were, and the proof cache stores the decisions with a result. build.py and economics.py read the data and fall back to the notes for an outcome from before the field; their patterns never matched the two notes a summary writes. sharedHelpers still means a helper proved equal on every input.

### Bind a proof to the class file a JVM loads: one selection in the checker, observed by a JVM, compared at launch

[`9b801632c2f8`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/9b801632c2f8bb2942cfd59d9a2ebdfbf0a3b4e7) · [log `1d12152af629`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/e61d882b-5ef7-428e-90df-ffe709ac6962/1d12152af62921a2af7da339fb787b2b9b71bf91e41ef9ef1e6cfa48f132e014.jsonl.gz)

Part 2 of llm-dlc/loops/lib-architecture-fast-follow.md. Two JARs that differ only in how the manifest spells Multi-Release's value (one line, or folded over two) load different classes on JDK 17, 21 and 25: the versioned entry of the first, the base entry of the second. The preparation took the base class of both; the Python launch guard and the Rust checker bound to release 21 took the versioned class of both, so on the folded JAR the checker refuted a property the JVM satisfies. Three parties each had a rule; now there is one selection, and it is held to a JVM.

lib/src/classpath.rs: ClassPath::bind says which class file stands for a class name on an ordered class path and the bound runtime (provider, JAR entry, SHA-256, how it was selected, every candidate, later holders), or a typed refusal with the candidates' digests and origins; every reader of class bytes in the checker goes through it. The manifest is read as the JDK's reader reads it, measured with fifteen spellings: a spelling on which that reading and the JAR specification's differ is ambiguous, and a class with a versioned entry in such a JAR is refused unless JVMCONTRACT_CLASS_OBSERVATIONS says which class file a JVM of the bound release loaded; an observation of other bytes than the rule's is a refusal with both digests. jvmcontract class-bindings answers for every side and class of a launch in one process, with whether the bound class file declares a method asked about and which entry stands for each logical name of a JAR.

examples/tools/targets/class_binding.py: the Python tools select nothing by rule. A class with one class file is read as before, and its prepared record is unchanged. A class the original artifact holds several class files of is bound at preparation by LoadedClasses on each JDK the artifact runs on (classSha256, jarEntry, classObservation); JDKs that load different bytes, another code source, or bytes no class file has are refused with both digests. Parameter lookup and every reader of a prepared entry class take the bound entry (runtime.bound_class). The native launch guard asks the checker for its bindings, one process whatever the sides and classes, and compares provider and digest with the prepared ones; the equivalence route extracts a JAR by the checker's own logical entries. A native-selector task asks once, whatever its number of selectors. runtime_jar.effective_entries stays as an inventory view for the upgrade review's tools, with the measured rule.

### Make array induction a library method: lib/python/jvm_array_induction.py, called on a bound method and a rule (verification pending)

[`b2718e6e9031`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/b2718e6e9031e40b80be969965f1b34e7d83ed47) · [log `1d12152af629`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/e61d882b-5ef7-428e-90df-ffe709ac6962/1d12152af62921a2af7da339fb787b2b9b71bf91e41ef9ef1e6cfa48f132e014.jsonl.gz)

The third part of the brief llm-dlc/loops/lib-architecture-fast-follow.md. The proof by induction over a compiled array loop was 696 lines inside one example tool. The method now lives in lib/python/jvm_array_induction.py: prove(javap, class_file, name, descriptor, rule, work, seconds) walks the method's disassembly, writes the obligations of the declared rule as one SMT query and reads Z3's answers, and knows no example, sidecar, revision or record. Reading a class file's methods from javap is lib/python/jvm_disassembly.py, which the schedule and monitor experiments now import instead of the proof method's module. examples/tools/targets/array_induction.py is left as the adapter: it finds the declared contract, takes the revision, prepares the artifacts, refuses a class whose initializer the rule does not qualify, and publishes the record. Cell width comes from the descriptor and the rule from the contract, with no switch on an example.

A record made from now on (java-array-induction-result/v2) names the rule implementation under rules: each file of the rule and the adapter by digest, and one digest over them. The fifteen stored records keep rulesSha256, the digest of the adapter file when it held the method too, and are read as before; rules_of reads either format. No stored record was rewritten and none was added.

The organic benchmark's baseline fingerprint and frozen export (lib/benchmark/organic-java/run.py) listed paths under lib/src, lib/models and examples/tools only, so code under lib/python was outside both. They are now versioned inventories that a pin names (inputs): a pin without the key is inventory 1 and is fingerprinted and exported exactly as before; inventory 2, for a new baseline, adds lib/python and verification/layout.py, which the example tools load at import (an export without it did not start since the process-plumbing run). The existing pin is unchanged.

Verified: each of the five declared contracts (336 first-any-length; 337 fill-any-length, caller-any-length and the negative control caller-extra-any-length; 346 first-any-length with 64-bit cells) proved again through the extracted method and compared with its stored record differs in no field: obligations with expected and obtained answers, widths, class digests, bytecode, certificate digest, status. The control stays unresolved on 'caller read follows from the proved frame' (expected unsat, obtained sat). That comparison is a new mode, build.py NNN --array-induction CONTRACT --compare, which writes nothing to the example; job 20261121-220624-array-induction-through-the-library-meth runs the five at this commit. New tests: lib/python/test_jvm_array_induction.py (6: a search compiled in the test, established for int and long cells, not established when it reads past the end, refused for a rule it does not fit), examples/tools/targets/test_array_induction.py (3) and lib/benchmark/organic-java/test_run.py (4: the pinned revision exported by its inventory has the pin's 224 files and fingerprint; a change to the extracted module alone changes inventory 2's fingerprint and not inventory 1's; a frozen export run with python3 -I loads its own reader and rules). test_costs.py run --changed passed 43 of 43, and examples 336, 337, 346, 342 and 343 pass validate_example.py.

### Add a setup phase to single-agent runs: a setup agent prepares a brief, and its notes go into the brief

[`8c34dda527cf`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/8c34dda527cfdf5146519c7ca7657c32a10bd614) · [log `174dbae8ebdd`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/e61d882b-5ef7-428e-90df-ffe709ac6962/174dbae8ebdd6decd08e3ef8e9bc8d106e01ad7667d3ace52b2a69cb4485cea7.jsonl.gz)

single_run.py setup NAME --brief FILE starts a setup agent (Claude Opus 5.5 at high effort by default) whose two texts come from the new llm-dlc/loops/setup-agent-template.md, with the brief and its record filled in. The agent only fetches, pins, verifies and builds what the brief needs, records it, and ends its record with a '## Setup Agent Notes' section for the domain agent. single_run.py notes NAME [--to FILE] puts that section into the brief and any other copy of it, replacing an earlier one, so a second run changes nothing. The /single-agent-run skill gains --setup and a 'A setup phase' section (when to use it, the drift signals for answering stop, waiting on its jobs, and the handover to the domain run), and llm-dlc/README.md describes it.

The template carries the lessons of the first setup pass (2026-11-22, the Spring and Java data brief): a built-in way to wait on jobs, checked substitution for public repositories that have gone away (and no assuming that an artifact exists elsewhere), a private GNUPGHOME whose agent is stopped at the end, and that other sessions' memory notes are not instructions. Verified with three new tests in test_single_run.py (the template's texts, the notes section's extraction and replacement, and a real setup run on the stand-in client through to notes in two copies of a brief), and test_costs.py run --changed: test_single_run, test_brief_run, test_conductor, test_prove_loop and test_watch all pass.

### 1. 2026-11-17 12:44 UTC

> Explore `/run-brief` and describe all options that can be passed when invoking a run to me

**Reply:**

`/run-brief` takes four arguments. Its signature, from `.claude/skills/run-brief/SKILL.md`:

```
/run-brief [--no-foundation] [--unattended] [--summary-interval SECONDS] <NAME | llm-dlc/loops/NAME.md>
```

| Option | What it does |
|---|---|
| **`<brief>`** (required) | The one brief to run, given by name (`domain-advances`) or by file (`llm-dlc/loops/domain-advances.md`). If the request doesn't clearly name one brief, the watcher asks before starting anything. A brief whose status is already `done` isn't run. |
| **`--no-foundation`** | Skips stage 2, the Fable 5.2 session that builds the shared groundwork and updates the plan before the streams start. Stage 2 is also skipped without this flag if a foundation has already landed or a stream's workspace already exists, because that means an earlier run is being continued. |
| **`--unattended`** | Tells the watcher you're away for the whole run. It doesn't bring you anything it can decide and record itself. A question only you can answer is recorded as an open decision (`decisions.py record`, state `open`), and the rest of the run carries on around it. This also covers test failures after a merge, or a foundation that changed what the brief is for: these become open decisions instead of stopping the run. |

### 2. 2026-11-17 13:13 UTC

> There seems to be issues with `RUN_STREAMS_WATCHER` in my latest feature brief, that is distracting agents from their goal. Check tmux win0 for watcher and da-* windows for other agents. Is this something we can fix without affecting the work in progress? We can look into a more strategic fix after it's done.

**Reply:**

Yes, it's fixed, and nothing that is running was changed. From each stream's next turn on, its sessions see `RUN_STREAMS_WATCHER` as empty, so the leaking test can no longer reach your watcher.

**What I found:** The watcher (win 0) had already worked this out and fixed the test on the main line (`smxzwqlr`). The four streams branched before that fix, so their copy of `test_brief_run.py` still passes the variable on. Whenever a stream ran its tests, the test's made-up run posted fake "merge stream a/b?" questions to the real watcher, then hung or failed. So far 11 or more questions have come in, all answered `leave`. The da-* windows show the cost: preservation, challenge and state each stopped to diagnose the failure and rerun the test with the variable unset.

**The fix:** I added `.claude/settings.local.json` to each stream workspace (state, evidence, preservation, challenge). It sets `RUN_STREAMS_WATCHER` to empty for that workspace's Claude sessions.
- **Nothing running is touched.** `run-streams.sh` keeps its own copy of the variable, so merge and blocked questions from the real streams still reach the watcher. Only the sessions it starts lose it, and nothing they run needs it.
- **Takes effect at each stream's next turn.** The loop starts a fresh `claude -p` for every turn, and that process reads the file. Turns already in progress keep the old value until they end.

Every evidence turn since then has been clean.

**All four streams now see the variable empty.** I checked the live processes: the shell inside each stream session that had one open (state, challenge, evidence) has `RUN_STREAMS_WATCHER` set to empty. Claude Code reloaded the setting partway through state's turn, which began before the fix, so streams don't have to wait for their next turn. Preservation had no shell open when I looked. Its turn began at 13:16:10, 33 seconds before the fix, and it's the only one I couldn't confirm directly.

**I looked for other variables that could leak the same way and found none.** The one with the same risk is `LOOP_CONDUCTOR`, each stream's channel to the watcher, which is still set in their shells. Its four question folders have no stray questions. In the streams' copy of the tests, `test_prove_loop.py` removes it before starting anything. `run-streams.sh` sets its own value for the loops it starts, which covers `test_brief_run.py`. **The watcher's framing doesn't hold up.** Preservation went 43 minutes without a commit, from 13:47 to 14:30. Only about 7 of those minutes went on the failing gap-scan test, starting at 14:23. Before that it made real progress:
- It modelled warning-level logging in the checker, with countermodels it ran on a real JVM.
- It deliberately weakened its own soundness check to confirm the tests would catch it.
- It modelled `String.valueOf(Object)` for a string or null argument.
- It probed example 287 at the claim's real bound and reached both versions' bcrypt. The probe failed there in the way the brief predicted.

**What made the test failure a subtle mistake:**
- The checker asks "can I run this call?" in two places: a scan that only sees the bytecode, and the engine, which sees the argument values. Both read one shared list of modelled calls.
- The agent added `String.valueOf(Object)` to that list. That made the scan claim the call is handled for every argument, when the engine only handles a string or null.
- It was following the entry next to it: `Pattern.compile` is already on the list, though it is also only modelled for some arguments.
- An existing test about 2,000 lines away holds the stricter rule. That test, not the model, caught the unsound change.

### 9. 2026-11-17 18:13 UTC

> Summarize I010 for me in the context of the running preservation stream

**Reply:**

## I010: a soundness hole in preservation's relational mechanism

**In one line:** the code the checker treats as "the same in both versions" can miss code that is actually different. When it does, it can prove two versions agree when a JVM shows they don't.

### The mechanism it breaks

Preservation's central result, the ties in commit `owrsowqm` (`lib/src/bmc/ties.rs`), works like this. When both versions run a loop the checker can't unroll fully, the checker summarizes it. If the two sides start the loop with the same **key**, they get one shared set of values rather than independent ones. That shared set is what removed 287's spurious counterexample. The key has three parts:
1. the code: a fingerprint of the method and everything it reaches;
2. the static fields of the classes that code uses;
3. the reachable objects, by class.

All three come from one function, `reach` in `lib/src/shared.rs`. **It skips every call whose owner is a JDK class**, on the reasoning that "the JDK is the same in both versions". That's true of the JDK's own code, but a call through a JDK interface (`IntUnaryOperator`, `Runnable`, `Comparator`, `Object.toString`) can run *application* code. That code is then in no fingerprint, its private helpers are in no class comparison, and the static fields it reads are in no key.

The timing works: preservation still has the 289/290 rerun (I011) and 287's new wall at `BCrypt.key` ahead of it, so it's likely hours from starting 307.

### Why 307 deserves a look first

307 looks like "the same technique, a second time", but its shape is different from 287 in ways that matter:

1. **The change sits exactly where the checker is weakest.**
   - The old version calls `password.getBytes("UTF-8")` inside a `try` that turns `UnsupportedEncodingException` into `AssertionError`. The new one calls `getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8)`.
   - The checker models only the second form (`lib/src/bmc/bytes.rs`), so 307's first stop will be at the old version's conversion.
   - Showing the two agree on every UTF-16 string (lone surrogates become `?`, a NUL counts, a null password throws `NullPointerException`) needs facts about the JDK. "UTF-8" is always supported, and both forms replace bad input the same way.
   - Modelling those facts loosely would produce a false proof in exactly the place the claim is about. That's the real soundness risk.

2. **There's a fork in the approach, and the brief points down the costlier branch.**
   - Step 6 says "by the same technique": run both versions' bcrypt, related by the ties.

### 13. 2026-11-17 19:04 UTC

> I'll check with the watcher on that. Does our current framework support companion claims? Any examples?

**Reply:**

Yes, in two senses. The second is the one that matters here.

### 1. Companion examples: a link only

`target.json` has `identity.companions` for related examples, such as a CVE's negative example and its positive one. 307 and 287 name each other this way, as do 305↔285 and 306↔286, and a unit test (`CompanionTest` in `examples/tools/targets/test_packets.py`) checks that each pair names the other. Nothing else uses the link: no evidence or verdict passes between companions.

### 2. Companion claims inside one example: the `parent` field

A task can name a `parent` task. The schema (`examples/schema/target.schema.json`) describes it as "a narrower diagnostic or derived claim: the task it is derived from, which stays unresolved." The rules are spelled out in `examples/tools/targets/workflow_handoff.py`:
- A frozen claim stays as it is. "A semantically changed proposal is a new claim with a parent link, for review."
- "A narrower kernel or a surrogate is a separate task with its own claim and explicit correspondence work; it never discharges this task's obligation without a checked connection."
- A gap closes only when the parent's *unchanged* claim is rerun and decided.

**The one example in use is 287's guard lemma:**
- **Parent** (`vulnerable-security` / `fixed-security`, `claims/overlong-candidate-rejected.json`): the public claim about `BCryptPasswordEncoder.matches` on a candidate String.

- **What would fix it:**
  - Now: run a stream's tests under a memory cap of their own, as challenge's inbox item I003 says.

**Reply:**

Claude-to-Codex messaging failed because typing into another agent's terminal is exactly what the permission system blocks. I'd fix this with a proper channel rather than by loosening permissions.

## What happened

- The session in window 2 (Fable, building the single-agent run, "brief 00") tried to message the interactive Codex in window 9 by pasting text into its tmux window. The command shown starts with `tmux capture-pane`, then builds a long message, presumably to type in with `send-keys`.
- **Auto mode's permission check denied it.** The reason text is cut off in the pane, so I can't quote it. But typing free-form text into another agent's interactive terminal looks like injecting instructions into a session someone else controls, and that's what the check is there to stop.
- **Claude-to-Claude messaging worked earlier because `SendMessage` is a sanctioned channel.** Codex isn't a Claude session, so `SendMessage` can't reach it.
- **It's fragile even when allowed.** Pasted multi-line text can garble, the paste can land while Codex is busy or you're typing in that window, and screen-scraping truncates. There's also no structured reply.

I'd **not** add an allow rule for `tmux send-keys` into agent windows. It removes a safeguard to keep a fragile channel. And having another session do it for you would get round your permission setting, which shouldn't happen either.

**There's one exception I should have avoided.** Running `jj log` and `jj diff` inside the worker's workspace makes jj **snapshot that workspace's working copy**, which is a write to the repository's operation log. The op log shows two snapshots caused by my reviews:

| Time | My command | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| 15:37:39 | `jj log -r 'mwmkmrmr::@' …` | recorded the worker's edits so far into its uncommitted change |
| 15:54:59 | the same, in this last check | the same |

My other `jj` commands found nothing new to record, so they left no operation.

**Impact:** harmless this time. A snapshot only records the files already on disk into the worker's uncommitted change, which its own next `jj` command does anyway, and nothing went stale or conflicted. But it isn't strictly read-only. If it had landed at the same moment as one of the worker's jj operations, it could have left a stale working copy for the worker to clean up.

**For later reviews**, I'll add `--ignore-working-copy` to every `jj` command in another session's workspace, which reads without snapshotting. I used it for the op-log check just now. Going further, I'll read the worker's uncommitted state only from its own log (`loop.log`) and the files on disk.

### 73. 2026-11-20 18:47 UTC

> I've sent a message to Codex for next cycle. Is there any way to message agent:agent within the current session? I thought this was added before, to ensure like:like capabilities from Claude Code.

**Reply:**

No: nothing can reach the Codex worker in the middle of a cycle. The parity work gave Codex the same hooks, permissions and tracing as Claude Code, plus a way for Claude sessions to consult Codex, but no message delivery into a running Codex turn. Your change to the continue message (recorded at 18:46, "by a person, from their terminal") is the right channel for a single run, and it takes effect at the start of the next cycle.

## What exists today

| Channel | Direction | When it arrives | Use for a running loop worker |
|---|---|---|---|
| Continue message (`single_run.py message`, yours only) | You → worker | Next cycle | **Yes.** This is the intended way to steer. |
| `ask_codex.py ask` | Claude → Codex, as a question and answer | At once, but in a **forked** thread | No. It consults a copy of the session, and never writes to the thread a worker or person is using. |
| `ask_codex.py note` (via `codex queue`) | Any → a Codex thread | That thread's next turn | Not for loops. It's meant for a session a person has open. For a loop worker the next turn is the next cycle, and it would bypass the rule that the continue message is yours alone. |
| `ask_codex.py mail send/list/read` | Any session ↔ any session, as files | Only when the receiver checks its mailbox | Not in practice. Nothing tells a loop worker to check, so mail sits unread. |
| Stream inboxes (`inbox.py`) | Conductor → stream, in multi-stream runs | Each cycle | Not wired for single-agent runs. |

### 84. 2026-11-20 23:53 UTC

> Why is it using Z3? Can you expand on this?

**Reply:**

Z3 is used because the native checker and JBMC can't prove anything "for every array length". Both are bounded checkers: they unroll a loop a fixed number of times and treat an array as a fixed number of cells. The best they can say is "correct for arrays up to N". The last campaign's claims asked for any legal length, up to 2^31−1: Guava `Ints.indexOf` and `Longs.indexOf` (336), and `Arrays.fill` over a range (337). That needs a proof by induction, and those obligations need a solver that understands arrays. Z3 does.

## How `array_induction.py` works

It does the classic loop proof (Floyd–Hoare style) over the compiled bytecode:

1. **Read the method** from the exact class file, using the pinned JDK's `javap`.
2. **Cut the loop at its head** and attach an invariant. For `indexOf` the invariant reads: `0 ≤ i ≤ length`, the heap is unchanged, and no element before `i` equals the target.
3. **Turn the loop into separate checks that contain no loop:**
   - the entry establishes the invariant;
   - each pass through the loop body keeps it;
   - each `return` gives the right answer;
   - every array access is in bounds;
   - the loop counter strictly decreases, so the loop terminates.
4. **Write each check in SMT-LIB using arrays and 32/64-bit integers** (the `QF_ABV` logic). The array is a symbolic array, and the claim "for every k" is checked by asking whether some `k` can break it, so no quantifiers are needed. Z3 must answer `unsat` (no counterexample) to every check.

The project settings denied it. Nothing malfunctioned: `.claude/settings.json` has this deny rule:

```
"deny": [ ..., "Bash(*reviewed-findings.json*)", ... ]
```

That pattern blocks **any** shell command whose text mentions `reviewed-findings.json`, read-only ones included. While checking your merge, the watcher ran this:

```
jj diff --from qzszlspr --stat llm-dlc/allowlist.json llm-dlc/reviewed-findings.json
```

It was checking whether the merge changed any approved allow-list entry or reviewed finding. The CLAUDE.md exception for merges requires checking that approved allow-list entries are unchanged. The rule matched the filename, so the command was denied.

**What happened, in order:**
1. A compound command (`sync.py regenerate`, `jj resolve --list`, that `jj diff`, and a Python comparison of the allow list) was denied, twice: once plain and once with `cd` in front.
2. The `jj diff` on its own was denied, twice as well. That second pair is the "2 actions not run".
3. The watcher then did the allow-list comparison without naming `reviewed-findings.json`. It found no approved entry changed, and went on to commit the merge. That commit is the one-time rescan for the new bucket-token rule, which takes several minutes.

**What it gains:**
1. **Commits stay fast.** Once a commit is on `develop`, the new `checkpoint` code marks it immutable for jj. It sets `immutable_heads()` to include `develop@origin` at repo level. From then on `sync.py commit` stops re-stamping trailers on it, so the 206-commit, 5½-minute problem from VF-053 can't build up again as long as checkpoints keep happening.
2. **Pushing is cheap and needs no human gate.** A checkpoint skips the default run, trace rendering and log upload. It only scans the new objects and pushes forward only, never with force. Your decision 1 already authorizes later checkpoints "under the new command's checks", so the watcher can checkpoint at cycle ends without asking.
3. **Another agent or machine can read the code** while runs continue, which is the brief's main outcome.

**What it doesn't fix:** the watcher still can't do the merge itself. It was refused permission for `jj new` merges, which is why you had to run this one from your terminal.

## Gotchas

1. **Every later checkpoint of the run's work needs a new merge.**
   - After this push, `develop` will point at the merge commit on the default line.
   - The plumbing agent keeps committing on its own line, which doesn't descend from that merge. A checkpoint of the agent's revision will be refused: "does not descend from develop: merge or rebase onto it first".

### 116. 2026-11-21 18:53 UTC

> How would you expand upon run 7's three question tests for the new brief? Let's try to keep it concise and high-level, or if minimal benefit just leave it as is.

**Reply:**

Run 7's test needs adapting, not just reusing. Its third question, "is a claim closer to decided?", doesn't fit a refactor. Lib-architecture is about one interpretation of proof output, binding checks to the class bytes that actually ran, and promoting array induction into `lib`. So the stop rule has to be about consumers switched over, not claims decided. Same shape, three questions:

1. **Consolidating, or adding a parallel path?** Does the cycle replace a duplicate interpretation and remove the old one, for example the Python class reader alongside Rust's, or ad hoc parsing of Rust's output? Or does it add one more layer beside them? New code that leaves both old paths in use doesn't count as progress.
2. **Do verdicts stay the same?** Results that agreed before must be unchanged on a sample of existing examples. Each disagreement the brief names gets a test that reproduces it first, then passes.
3. **Is a real consumer using it?** Has at least one of the three changes reached the end: a real consumer reads the new contract, or an example proves through the promoted array-induction code in `lib`? **Two cycles in a row of scaffolding with no consumer switched means stop.**

The benefit is worth it. Without the change, the watcher would judge question 3 against claims, which this brief doesn't move much, and might stop a healthy refactor or keep a stalled one going.

### 117. 2026-11-21 18:55 UTC

> What happens if Fable runs out of usage in Claude Code before the two briefs end? I have credits, will they start to be used seamlessly to avoid disruption?

**Reply:**

**Short answer: your credits are only used seamlessly if extra usage is switched on, and I couldn't confirm that this works for our headless runs.**

**What the docs say:**
- **It's opt-in.** Turn it on in claude.ai under Settings → Usage, with a payment method and a monthly spend limit (`/usage-credits` in Claude Code opens that page). Once it's on, requests "switch to pay-as-you-go pricing on usage credits and keep working", and Claude Code shares the same limit. If it's off, the plan's included usage is all you get. ([extra usage](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/12429409-extra-usage-for-paid-claude-plans), [costs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/costs.md))
- **Fable has its own weekly limit on Max and Ultra**, separate from the shared session and weekly limits. The docs don't say clearly whether extra usage covers going past that Fable limit.
- **The monthly API credits included with Max can't be spent as usage credits.** If those are the credits you mean, they won't help here.
- **Headless `claude -p`, which our loop uses, isn't documented at the limit.** Waiting for the reset and continuing is documented only for interactive sessions, so a `-p` turn most likely just fails. ([errors](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/errors.md), [headless](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/headless.md))

## 1. Trusted kernel experiment (next, 19 KB)
**Question:** is an independently checked Java proof worth the effort?
- **The work:** build a small checker that accepts or rejects one precise claim about the real compiled bytes of Guava's `Ints.indexOf` (example 336). Then freeze the checker and measure what it costs to transfer it to `Longs.indexOf` (346). Example 337 is optional.
- **Two candidate routes, compared on the same theorem:** a Rust semantic checker and a Lean one. A SAT/LRAT certificate checker runs alongside as a cheaper comparison.
- **Controls:** a method that returns the correct answer but damages the heap, and a deliberately broken producer that swaps in a tautology. The experiment has to catch both.
- **Deliverable:** an evidence-based decision on whether to invest further.

**Setup weight: medium, and different from before.**
- **Toolchains:** Lean, plus CakeML's `cake_lpr` and `coch-demo` for LRAT checking, both from GitHub.
- **Pinned class bytes:** extracted from the Guava JARs.

Lean and its libraries can take several GB of disk, and there's 102 GB free. This is the first setup pass that installs proof-assistant toolchains rather than Java ones, so it's a good test of how general the setup template is.
